blocks.label: Introduction and learning outcomes on the hallmarks of cancer
blocks.content: So unfortunately, I'm going to have to start now. Otherwise, I'm going to sound like an auctioneer in this lecture because this is the longest lecture to get through. So we're going to have to pretty much start on time. And for those that drift in, so be it. So you've seen the cancer process in the tissue. You've heard from Professor Turner about the causes of cancer. You heard about genomic and genetic instability and how DNA damage can cause an acceleration of the process of tumorigenesis. Today, we're going to talk about mechanisms and kind of the hallmarks of cancer, which I'm sure you've come across before. But we're going to go through them and try and assign them to what we're seeing that happens in the tissues. Okay? So for today, the learning outcomes are as follows in terms of the hallmarks of cancer, which, as I said, we'll try to go through step by step. We'll explain how mutations in the individual genes are acting in the cancer pathways themselves, and how they contribute to hallmarks and how sometimes these mutations can contribute to multiple hallmarks. And we're going to use P53 as an example of a master regulator and how it controls a lot of things. It's, after all, the guardian of the genome. And we'll also see how clinicians can use these hallmarks for diagnostic purposes. Okay? So pretty straightforward what we're going to do today. And we're going to come back time and time again to this kind of our model, which as I've said and emphasized, is only one example of a tumor progression, and only because we can see the precursor stages from adenomas moving to adenocarcinomas, and we can sequence these things. As I said before, for many tumors, we don't really know what these pre-neoplastic states look like, and so it's difficult to map mutations onto them. So we have a timeline, and we also have a progression of mutations that occurs, and the consequences for the cells and the consequences for the tumor kind of outlined here. But what we don't understand is what are all these mutations doing. And so we'll try and go through what they're doing today and what that means for the tumor in terms of its functional properties, which have been very eloquently described for the past 26 years by this series of reviews that were published starting at the turn of the millennium by Doug Hanahan and Bob Weinberg, the Hallmarks of Cancers. I'm sure you've come across it. It has somehow, over the years, morphed into something that is more and more complicated, more and more difficult to, if you like, digest in one easy sitting. Probably unnecessarily so. I don't want you to get overwhelmed by all the different things as they get added, because they are kind of describing similar things in different ways. So what we're going to do is we're going to stay with the kind of somewhat simpler version, a little bit more expanded than the six to these 10 hallmarks here. And you'll touch on these topics anyway. I don't want you to think that you're not learning up-to-date stuff in terms of what these things actually mean for tumors. And of course-- Ooh, there's a little bug here. Of course, you're always welcome to go off and read these things. But you'll see here that they, as I said, kind of have an overlapping effect on this loss of growth control. And remember what we're talking about when we're talking about cancer is the loss of the ability of the cells to understand who they are and what they're trying to do in terms of 3D tissue architecture, communication with the neighboring cells, and making up a functional tissue. Maybe we will take a tiny break while people come into the lecture theater. So this loss of growth control is a common feature, if you like, of all of these things. You could say that loss of growth control is arising from all of these independent hallmarks here. So let's kind of go through them as I said.
blocks.why: The lecturer frames the lecture by outlining learning outcomes, relating to prior lectures, and introducing the Hanahan and Weinberg framework of cancer hallmarks.

blocks.label: Growth signal autonomy and insensitivity to antigrowth signals
blocks.content: So we'll start with these first two, independence for growth stimulation and resistance to growth inhibitory signals, these two pretty much at the top. So again, coming on to where we left off on the last lecture, one of you, I can't remember who it was, asked about the order of these mutations, and does every tumor have these? And what I had said in answer to that is this is really the most efficient way that you can get yourself to a colorectal cancer. The order of these mutations, when they happen, and whether or not specific mutations occur in particular genes is different for every tumor that arises. But if you look at the components of this, like beta-catenin deregulation here, you'll see that the preponderance of different mutations is different. So you have some 4% of tumors will have axin mutations, 15% beta-catenin, and so on and so forth. Similarly for receptor tyrosine kinases, there are so many receptor tyrosine kinases that this is just kind of a class of activity that's being mutated here, as well as downstream signal transducers here in terms of PI3 kinase, Ras, and Raf. Similarly for TGF-beta, you'll have the receptor and the transducer, and then we'll come on to P53 later. So these signaling molecules here at the front are the ones that would be mutated and are the sensors of the external environment and kind of telling the cell what it should be doing. So what does that look like? These are receptor tyrosine kinases here on the cell membrane. These can also be Wnt receptors or TGF-beta receptors. They're here on the cell surface, and they signal through, if you like, a mid-level set of protein signaling cascades that will cascade through to signal into the nucleus. And the effect on the cell is receiving these extracellular signals, and they will either promote proliferation to enter into the cell cycle or prevent death by increasing the survival capacity of the cells. So what does that look like in terms of APC? Because this is the main gene that we've been talking about in terms of its function here. So here's the Wnt receptors. The specific names are not so important, just to know that these are receptors on the cell surface. And without the ligand to bind to the receptor, you have the formation of this degradation complex here. This is a very, very large protein complex. APC is here. Axin is actually the scaffold. It recruits GSK-3 beta, which is a kinase, which can phosphorylate beta-catenin. Phosphorylated beta-catenin is easily recognized by an E3 ubiquitin ligase, which promotes its polyubiquitination and degradation. So in the absence of ligand, beta-catenin is very rapidly destroyed. This is a very quick turnover, so the half-life of the protein is very short. When the ligands are present, these ligands can bind to the receptor, and this inhibits this degradation complex. So you no longer have phosphorylation of beta-catenin, and now beta-catenin levels are stabilized in the cytoplasm. They move into the nucleus here, and they displace Groucho, which is a repressor of this TCF. And there's a heterodimerization between TCF and beta-catenin here. And now this transcription factor dimer, heterodimer, becomes active, and it promotes the transcription of a whole swathe of genes that's involved in proliferation. So that is what it looks like. So you have to get a signal through the Wnt signaling pathway in order for the cells to proliferate. And it's transduced through beta-catenin and its stabilization. So the mutations that occur, we've already talked about mutations in beta-catenin or axin. You saw that was 4%, that was 80% of sporadic cancers. But you can also get mutations in beta-catenin that prevent it from being phosphorylated. And if it can't be phosphorylated, its levels rise, and again, it can move into the nucleus. You can also get mutations in TCF4, which elevate its concentration, and so if you have more of this, you can get better signaling and better transcription. Right? So these are some of the mutations that would lead to increased beta-catenin activity in these cancer cells. Similarly, receptor tyrosine kinases, there are a whole bunch. We're using here the example of ErbB. Remember I told you about these kinds of cellular proto-oncogenes being discovered as viral oncogenes originally. This is an example of them. So again, they bind their ligand, in this case epidermal growth factor, and then they signal. The signal of the ligand binding to the receptor is transduced through these different pathways. One of them is Ras signaling. BRAF is a kinase. It will phosphorylate all of the MAP kinase signals. This is the mitogen-activating protein kinase cascade. And then again, this signals for proliferation and survival. Similarly, you have PI3 kinase. This is the catalytic alpha subunit that will become activated. It takes PIP3, which is a phospholipid in the cell membrane. It takes it from being doubly phosphorylated to being triply phosphorylated. This becomes the messenger that allows activation through AKT, and again, signals for proliferation and survival, also simultaneously suppressing signals for apoptosis. Right? So there is a phosphatase that will take this phosphate off and take it back down to the non-signaling PIP2 intermediate. So what are the mutations that happen? You can get activation of Ras. You should be very familiar with this point mutation that will activate Ras. There are also activating mutations of Raf that can happen. Again, this results in more sustained signaling through the MAP kinase cascade. Alternatively, you can have mutations that activate PI3 kinase that will increase the rate of PIP3 being formed, or you can have mutations that take out the phosphatase, which keep the levels of PIP3 high in the cell, and this results in more sustained signaling through AKT, more proliferation, more survival for the cancer cells. So this kind of mutations can occur, as you saw in that big list, all over this cascade. And so they're all present within colorectal cancer. So which pathway or which mutation specifically occurs is not as important as the fact that these pathways are activated in cancer. Okay? So it can kind of also hint at where you might want to try and treat your cancer, what types of inhibitors you could use, and we'll have that as the problem-solving exercise in the practicals at the end of this week. So what kind of inhibitors might you think about using if you have sustained signaling in these pathways? And the last one to mention, which was number three in that list of four, was TGF-beta receptors, which actually have normally an inhibitory signal. And when these proteins are, or rather genes are inhibited, they remove an inhibitory signal, which allows increased survival. Okay? So these types of signaling cascades should be pretty straightforward conceptually in kind of what they're doing for the cancer cell. The upshot is this promotion of proliferation and increasing of survival.
blocks.why: This section explains how mutations in upstream signaling cascades, including Wnt/APC/beta-catenin, RTKs, and TGF-beta, deregulate proliferation and survival.

blocks.label: Differentiation block in leukemia and colorectal carcinoma
blocks.content: So we'll move on to something that is slightly less evident or less obvious from some of the mutations that you would see, but you have to look a little bit more carefully to appreciate what's happening to the cancer cell itself. And this is this differentiation block. So most cells, when they undergo a particular differentiation to a lineage, by the time they're getting to their terminally functional state, they will withdraw from the cell cycle, and they will execute their primary function. So cancer cells often have this differentiation block, and you saw it a little bit in the leiomyoma, or leiomyosarcoma. I think that, yes, where you saw the muscle cells had some muscle proteins being expressed but weren't fully terminally differentiated. So they had a block to their differentiation. It's easier to conceptualize this in the hematopoietic system because hematopoiesis has been studied for decades and decades and decades, partly because the tissue is so easy to access. So this is just a cartoon, a very, very basic cartoon of hematopoiesis, which starts from a stem cell and obviously goes through different lineage specifications. There's a common myeloid progenitor cell, there's a common lymphoid progenitor cells, and you can get B and T cells from the lymphoid, and you get all the different mature myeloid cells that arise from the myeloid lineage from that progenitor cell. So there are proliferative diseases that can occur, and mutations that will allow this expansion of the myeloid progenitor cell, and this results in this chronic myeloid leukemia. But there is no block to differentiation in this disease. And what you see instead is a huge increase in the number of granulocytes in the blood, but also a commensurate decrease in the number of mature cell types, including in the lymphoid lineage, but also in the myeloid lineage. So you do see an increased number of neutrophils and monocytes in this disease condition. Right? So you can tell that even though there's a hyperproliferation here, there's no block to differentiation. When there is a block to differentiation, it looks very, very different in the cell, and this is acute myeloid leukemia. And what you then see is a huge number of these common myeloid progenitors filling the blood. Right? And they don't differentiate, so they have a very blast-like appearance to them. So when this happens in the lymphoid lineage, when there's a differentiation block, say, for example, in this progenitor cell, this is an acute B lymphoblastic leukemia. And you'd have to subtype it to understand that it's a pro-B cell. And then these pro-B cells fill the blood as well. There isn't an expansion of the common lymphoid progenitor in the way that there was the common myeloid progenitor. No proliferative disease there, but the differentiation block can happen in pro-B cells, and it can also happen in a mature lineage as well. So then this is what you see chronic lymphocytic leukemia, where a mature B cell is hyperproliferative. And how we know that that is a mature B cell is because we can see VDJ recombination in the immunoglobulin locus. So we know that it has gone through the differentiation process to become a B cell. Right? And this is also the evidence that not all cancers are arising from stem cells or progenitor cells, because this is a mature cell type. It makes immunoglobulin. And similarly, the expansion of plasma cells is multiple myeloma, where those cells are pumping out a lot of antibody into the circulation. So you can definitely get cancers in what would be considered terminally differentiated cells. Right? So it's quite easy to conceptualize this because we know, and we can see, and we can genotype, and we can look at the expression of different genes in the maturing lineages to understand where exactly has it gone wrong in this cancer, in this leukemia. But I want you to also to be able to appreciate in the context of a carcinoma. So this is what this can look like in colorectal carcinoma. Right? So what the differentiation block would look like. And we'll go back to Wnt signaling, right? Because again, it's the most common mutation in sporadic colorectal cancer. And you will be familiar with the histology of a normal small intestine here. And again, you have the villi with the very, very nice colonic epithelium here, nice regular architecture, all the nuclei lining up at the basement. And then what I want you to appreciate here is that, again, that nice regular architecture is here, this crypt region. So what is happening in the crypt is that this is where the stem cells are, and this is where they are expanding and differentiating. So the way that that works is that the stem cell compartment, for the most part, doesn't divide very often. It's a slowly turning over compartment in terms of proliferation. But as it enters the, if you like, the differentiation lineage, and remembering that a stem cell here is multipotent in terms of the cells that it can make, so it has the capacity to code for enterocytes. It can also be self-renewing goblet cells. There are some kind of endocrine cells that are here. So a lot of different cell types can be specified by the stem cells in the crypt. But the first step is to turn into, if you like, or differentiate into this transit amplifying cell here, where it's very, very rapidly dividing. And as it goes up the villus, it starts to differentiate into one of these different cell types, and if you like, execute its function. Enterocytes are absorptive cells. Goblet cells are secreting the mucin, which you've seen. And then by the time it gets all the way up to the tip here, it's going to be shed into the lumen. So the whole thing takes about, I'd say, three to five days, before the cells have gone from differentiating to exiting in the lumen of the intestine and being shed. Right? So this is what the epithelial renewal looks like in the intestine. And this is a very nice experiment that was done some time ago to look at the inactivation of APC in the crypt. So then you're like, "Well, what's going to happen if we make the mutation that is the first initiating cancer mutation, at least in that little diagram, in this population of cells?" So what happens then is that you see that there's a massive expansion of this crypt region. So now you guys, being expert histologists of the intestine, can see that this nice architecture that you had that was one cell thick of that colonic epithelium is now much more crowded. Right? You see that there's at least two or three or four cells thick here, that you have an expansion. It's much more darkly stained. These cells probably are not differentiating as well as they could in terms of making their mucin, which is easy for you to see. And this would be a dysplastic situation here. So the cells are not differentiating particularly well. Right? And you'll see that-- is there anything else we want to see here? I guess this is what we can appreciate in terms of this lack of differentiation that arises from the Wnt mutation as well. So not only is Wnt controlling proliferation, it's also impacting on the capacity of these cells to differentiate. Okay?
blocks.why: This section examines how cancer cells fail to complete terminal differentiation, contrasting hematopoietic leukemias with dysregulated crypt architecture in the colon.

blocks.label: Evasion of apoptosis through p53 pathway alterations
blocks.content: So we're going to move on to resistance to apoptosis. God, I forgot to start this thing again. Okay, we're doing all right. Okay, so resistance to apoptosis. So what does that look like? So this is here in this fourth mutation that we know happens late in the process of making the tumor. Right? And we know this because these mutations only show up in the adenocarcinoma as opposed to in the adenoma. So we know these mutations are here early, and these mutations only show up late. So this loss, at least in this cartoon, of p53 happens later in this tumor. And that's probably-- Well, you can ask your supervisors about why that might happen in this specific tumor type. Yeah. Okay. So the mutations that are listed here are all involved in the regulation of p53. So p53 itself, you can just mutate it. MDM2 is the E3 ubiquitin ligase that degrades p53. So the mutations of MDM2 that are found would increase its activity. And so that would result in a reduced abundance of p53 in the cells. And p14ARF is the negative regulator of MDM2. So you can see that we have tumor suppressor genes, oncogenes, are the different types of mutations that you might get, all of which would lead to inactivation of the p53 function within this tumor. Okay. So what does that look like? This is just a very small part of the p53 pathway and just to show you what that would look like. So p53 is a transcription factor. It transactivates a whole host of genes, and one of the genes that it does transactivate is a protein called Bax. It's a pro-apoptotic protein, and what it does is that it can localize onto the outer mitochondrial membrane here, and when it manages to get to a high enough concentration, it can form a cluster, if you like, that results in mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization, which allows the release of cytochrome c into the cytoplasm. And this is an irreversible step. This is the penultimate step in apoptosis. Once you have caspase activation here, there's no going back in terms of apoptosis. Right? So this is an important regulator in terms of its localization and concentration on the mitochondrial outer membrane. So one of the proteins that opposes that is a protein called BCL2. BCL2 is named for B-cell lymphoma, actually. And it can be amplified in B-cell lymphomas. And it opposes the activity of Bax on the mitochondrial membrane by sequestering it away from itself so that it cannot multimerize and it cannot form this pore. Right? So the mutations that can occur can be of p53 itself, can be of Bax, so that either it isn't made or p53 doesn't transactivate it. And so in this way, the cell would become resistant to apoptosis induction by mutation of p53. You can also, as I said, get amplification of BCL2, and if you have a lot more of this, it outweighs or can sequester the Bax so that you never get that signal to apoptose. So there's a balance between the pro and the anti-apoptotic factors in the cell, but there is a point of no return once caspase activation goes that the cell will be committed to dying. Right? So there's a balance that needs to be found by the cell. Okay? So that's what p53 activity looks like, just one small part in terms of the last stages of apoptosis induction.
blocks.why: This section details the molecular mechanisms of apoptotic resistance involving p53 inactivation, MDM2 regulation, Bax permeabilization, and BCL2 overexpression.

blocks.label: Replicative immortality, telomeres, and senescence
blocks.content: So the last one that I will talk about or hallmark that I'm going to talk about with regard to loss of growth control has to do with this immortalization of tumor cells. Right? So, this is a concept that came about because of the Hayflick limit, which is something when people were trying to culture normal cells many years ago. And the term for this is the Hayflick limit. When you put cells in culture, and this was established, I think, with keratinocytes, and it differs from cell type to cell type. But I think this is done in keratinocytes from the skin. And you'll see that if you put adult keratinocytes in culture, you'll get about 50 doublings, population doublings before the cells stop growing in culture at all. And if you put fetal cells in culture, they will go for a little bit longer. And this contrasts with cancer cells, which can grow and divide in culture indefinitely. And of course, this was found to be due to the telomeres, which are, of course, the little structures at the very end of chromosomes here. Right? So this is hopefully something that you're familiar with. And the structure of the telomeres is depicted here in this cartoon. This is the sequence that you'll see at the very end, which is TTAGGG. And there's multiple repeats of this, totaling up to 15 kilobases of these repeats. And what happens at the very end is you have this structure called the T-loop, and this single-stranded piece of DNA can insert into this kind of triple DNA strand structure called the D-loop, which has a number of proteins that help to shelter the whole thing. That's why it's called shelterin, to prevent the nibbling away of this single-stranded DNA at the very end of the chromosomes. Right? So this is what this structure looks like, and this, of course, is necessary also to, A, to not trigger the DNA damage response, but also to protect these ends During also cell divisions, because in cell division, because of the structure, there is no way to copy this three prime overhang without the use of telomerase. So telomerase is an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase or reverse transcriptase, which was discovered, I think, about 30 years ago. It uses an RNA template to copy this last G overhang that's present at the end of chromosomes. So this is all very nice. But the telomeres, and this is kind of like the clock that determines how long your cells can grow in culture, they shorten by about 100 base pairs with every cell division. And actually, it's pretty simple math, because if the telomeres is about five to 10 kB in length, you get about 50 to 100 cell divisions before the telomeres are too short, and they trigger senescence in cells. Right? So this also jives very much with those numbers that you just heard in terms of the lifespan of keratinocytes or adult keratinocytes in culture. So these need to be made longer, otherwise the cells will trigger senescence, and that's what telomerase does. So in the context of normal biology, if you like, when the telomeres get too short, it triggers a DNA damage response, and you get cell cycle arrest, and the cells will enter senescence. So you can consider senescence as an anti-oncogenic kind of fail-safe for the cells. Right? So senescence has its own set of characteristics, and they're very easy to see. It's present in vivo, so it's definitely not something that's an artifact of tissue culture, of just growing cells in a plastic dish. And you'll get things like senescence-associated beta-galactosidase. You'll get heterochromatic foci. You get protection of the mitochondria. You get lots of these anti-apoptotic proteins that are embedded in the mitochondria to prevent apoptosis from happening. You get a large number of metabolic changes. There's a senescence-associated secretory phenotype. Lots of cytokines are secreted by the cells. And the cells are really pretty much in arrest because they have very high concentration of cell cycle inhibitors. So the cell looks like a giant fried egg in a dish, and it also looks like a giant fried egg in tissues. Right? So these are very highly metabolically active cells, and they are thought to also contribute to an aging phenotype. This is what stress looks like normally, not cancer, as we age. So in order for immortalization to occur, you pretty much have to try and bypass this effect, and restore telomere length, and telomere activity to the cell. So how does the cancer do this? Well, it has a number of mutations, and I've just put two of them up here to exemplify what happens. These mutations are not to the coding sequence of telomerase, because you need the telomerase to be an active enzyme. So these are actually the most common mutations that happen outside of a coding sequence in cancers. So lots of different cancers have these types of mutations, and these are point mutations within the promoter region that's upstream of the TERT open reading frame, that happen to create a binding site for the ETS family of transcription factors. So suddenly you have a point mutation here, and this becomes a better binding site for ETS transcription factors, and this causes an upregulation of the expression of TERT. You can get these somatically, so you can acquire these mutations, or there are people that are born with germline mutations in this promoter region that would have, if you like, higher activity of TERT. So TERT is normally not expressed in adults. You get some expression in the germline, obviously, to make your gametes. But it's pretty much not expressed in most cells, in the vast majority of cells. The other type of mutation that you can get, so these are point mutations. You can get promoter rearrangements, where a whole different part of a chromosome with a super enhancer can get translocated upstream of the promoter of TERT, and this results in increased transcription of this gene. And this is particularly the case for about a quarter of high-risk neuroblastoma cases, for example. Okay? So this is how a cancer cell would achieve higher levels of TERT. So I just want to say that senescent signaling is what we would call normal stress signaling. Right? So we've talked here about telomere shortening and damage. Right? So when it gets too short, it looks like an end that the telomerase cannot extend, and there's no telomerase anyway, and it triggers this DNA damage response. And the DNA damage response feeds through p53 to cause cell cycle arrest. Similarly, the DNA damage that we were talking about in the last lecture, things like double-stranded breaks and things like that, will all cascade through various sensors and all of the protein machinery that senses and checks and helps to repair the broken DNA. And again, this feeds through p53 to cause cell cycle arrest so that this repair can be effected, that there's enough time to do the repair, because we want to maintain genome integrity. Similarly, oncogene activation and things like Ros production cause hyperproliferation, things like Ras activation, and they also can cause replication stress and, as I said, can cause fragility and DNA damage at various sites when transcription and replication forks clash. And this can also, again, trigger p53 activation and cell cycle arrest. These are all normal features of p53 to guard your genome to make sure that your genome stays intact. Right? So things like when p53 is activated, it will increase the transcription of things like p- P21 or Bax, as we said, can either kill that cell off because it's damaged beyond repair or pause the cell cycle so that the cell can repair its DNA or make the cell senesce and just put it in a frozen state so that it can't transform any further. So these are all these safety mechanisms. And you'll remember that these are also the three things that I said that extrachromosomal DNA would trigger if the cell had a mitotic defect and had DNA, for example, located outside the nucleus. So P53 is very much important to trigger all of these different cell fates. They all sound like perhaps not such great things compared to just having good, healthy cells. But this is the mechanism that maintains genome integrity. Okay? So you'll see that we'll kind of leave this set of fairly straightforward to conceptualize how genetic mutations result in this hallmark to arise. Right? You can think of mutations that increase growth stimulation. You can think of things that block growth inhibition, et cetera. So I've told you about mutations that can lead to these hallmarks. We come to the other part of the list now, where it's a little bit harder to see how the mutations that you could just acquire will lead to these somewhat larger changes in the behavior of the cancer itself. We talked about genetic instability. I've told you about mutations that can occur, like DNA Pol E, et cetera, but I'm talking more about things like metabolic changes, angiogenesis, metastasis. And I won't talk about evasion of the immune response because Professor Turner is going to tell you about all of that in a separate lecture. Okay.
blocks.why: This section covers the Hayflick limit, telomere biology, TERT activation mechanisms, and how cells bypass senescence to achieve immortalization.

blocks.label: Metabolic reprogramming and oncometabolites
blocks.content: So we'll move on to metabolism, because this is a very important aspect of cancer and has been noticed for many, many years, especially this thing called the Warburg effect. And so the Warburg effect is the propensity of cancer cells to do aerobic glycolysis, which is to say that they take the glycolysis, and instead of using it in the Krebs cycle, they use it to ferment and to make lactate. And they do this obviously even in the presence of oxygen. So it's known as aerobic glycolysis. Okay? This was noticed back in the '30s, and Otto Warburg was the person that discovered this or described it very much. And he even thought that this was because the cancers had dysfunctional mitochondria, that they couldn't make use of the pyruvate at the end of glycolysis because there was something wrong with the mitochondria. But this really isn't the case. Right? So the mitochondria work just fine in cancer cells. There's no problem there. So it's been like a conundrum. Why would you go with this inefficient method of making just two ATPs instead of getting the 36 that you would get out of oxidative phosphorylation? Why would you do that? Well, it's pretty reductive to just think that two ATP is all you're getting, because there are other reasons why you might want to use this. And you could also just sort of say that cancer cells are very glucose greedy, right? So they often upregulate glucose transporters, and you can see this even on PET scans with cancer patients. And this is one of the things that, the hallmarks that we can use to help with diagnosis of cancers, and we can see where they are. So if you give patients a glucose analog, you can see that the tumors will light up because they're very glucose hungry on a scan. Right? So the reasons for why cancer cells undergo aerobic glycolysis have been a little bit hand-wavy, but probably are not incorrect in the sense that there are other very, very high biosynthetic demands that the tumor may have, and there are other signaling pathways that could arise from the use of glucose in this way. So these are kind of the reasons that are listed here. So what does that mean in terms of metabolic rewiring? Because this is kind of what you talk about. If you look at metabolism as a series of biosynthetic pathways, it's extremely complicated or complex, and also that they all feed into each other and things can take routes in different ways. So this kind of paper, I don't want you to look at this in too much detail, but it's to kind of give you a global overview of what's happening in cancer. And so this looks at signaling pathways, and where they're mutated, and these are the ones that you should recognize, things like Wnt and PI3 kinase, Ras and p53 and MYC. And you can see that in different cancers, different mutations predominate in different cancers. So everything is different. But looking at metabolic pathways, and here you can measure metabolite levels, and you can look at the gene expression of the genes that are involved in things like carbon metabolism, nucleotide metabolism, and lipid metabolism. You'll see that really the main change that you can see is that glycolysis is present, upregulated in almost all of these different cancers. So it's quite common in that regard. Whereas OXPHOS isn't. OXPHOS isn't always changed in cancers. Right? So really, the thing to kind of take away from this slide is that cancer does rewire particular cancers that derive from them to upregulate glycolysis, but that different tissues are still very different from each other in terms of their metabolism. So like a pancreatic cancer very much is similar in its metabolism to regular pancreas. Right? It doesn't suddenly have the metabolism of, say, a liver cell. So you can see the tissue of origin. Cells become, as it said here, hardwired for their specific metabolism. But cancer cells change that towards the use of glycolysis. Okay? Right. So the big question is, is this something that we can take advantage of other than for things just like diagnostics? ... a metabolic change a cause of cancer? Are we looking at genes that change things or is it just an effect? Right. And the answer is a little bit of both. They kind of feed into each other in terms of what they're doing. So there are mutations that have been discovered in genes in the Krebs cycle, for example. There are mutations in things like isocitrate dehydrogenase, fumarase, and succinate dehydrogenase. And these are mutations that, in the case of fumarase and succinate dehydrogenase, take out the activity of these enzymes. Right? In the case of isocitrate dehydrogenase, it's a change of function. Right? This is why I have them in different colors here. So the loss of function of fumarase and succinate dehydrogenase causes the metabolites preceding them, the substrates for these enzymes, to increase in concentration in the cell. So suddenly the cancer cell now has a large amount of succinate or fumarate within the cell. And in the case of isocitrate dehydrogenase, it changes the activity of that enzyme so that it produces this different product, which is an onco-metabolite. It's called R2-hydroxyglutarate. Right? So when you see R2-hydroxyglutarate in a cell or in a cancer, it's a biomarker of the fact that this isocitrate dehydrogenase is mutated. So then the question is, well, what do these metabolites do for the cancer cell? Right. So really you're talking about the dysregulation of these enzymes. You get much altered metabolism because you don't have things pumping through the Krebs cycle. And these different metabolites also participate in changes to enzymes that modify histone and DNA methylases. So they change the epigenome. Right? That is the big effect of these mutations. So it's not particularly clear which ones are the important drivers in tumor development, and that's kind of what's exemplified here. You can have oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes that are mutated, and you can also make onco-metabolite genes, as we were talking about here, and they will affect transcription of various downstream genes, as you can see here. And this causes a deregulation of metabolism. But what happens is that deregulation of metabolism goes back up, changes the epigenome, which then changes the expression of oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes, which are also involved in transcription again. And some of these genes here, like beta-catenin and Myc are master regulators of the genes that regulate metabolism. Right? So it's not just that these are direct metabolites in, for example, the Krebs cycle, but these genes are also-- Funny little fly. Myc regulates a whole bunch of different genes that are involved in metabolism as well. So it's pretty much something that you could see self-reinforcing and self-perpetuating and causing further and further deregulation. Okay? So again, it's a little bit less clear.
blocks.why: This section explores cancer cell metabolism, including aerobic glycolysis via the Warburg effect, biosynthetic demands, and the epigenetic effects of oncometabolites.

blocks.label: Induction of angiogenesis in tumor growth
blocks.content: Similarly for angiogenesis, right, in terms of what that does for the cell. So angiogenesis is a normal property of cells, right? So your vasculature, for the most part, is really quiescent, right? Most of your vasculature and the development of your vasculature occurs during embryogenesis. And your endothelium will turn over every, I don't know, 14 years. That's how slow-growing your vasculature is, except for the female reproductive cycles. So things like pregnancy, menstruation, there's lots of angiogenesis there. But for the most part, unless something pathological occurs, like you have a wound or you have hypoxia, there's not a lot of angiogenesis that occurs. So the hypothesis that was mooted, I think, about 30 years ago, was that in order for a tumor to actually grow, angiogenesis must occur. Because if you have some transformed cells here, there's a point that they get to where they need to have this switch in angiogenesis. They need to upregulate angiogenesis in order to call, if you like, for the endothelium to come to the area of hypoxia and innervate and bring oxygen and supplies to that tumor. So you need oxygen and nutrient perfusion via angiogenesis. And what that looks like is here. You'll see that here you have a little vessel, and you'll see that around it you have some live cells. But once you go past the oxygen diffusion in this tissue out here, you end up with necrotic tissue. So this tumor would never be able to grow unless angiogenesis occurred. Right? So it's a necessary part of tumor formation. Right? And you can see the same thing over here. Another vessel, another live bit, all this other dead bit around it. Okay? So the question is, when does it happen in tumor genesis? And the answer is potentially quite early. Right? It might be something, again, because it's a normal process that the cancer is taking advantage of in order for it to grow. It may just be that this happens much sooner than you think. So here you have normal skin. And again, we have here in a dotted line the basement membrane that we were talking about. You can see some hyperplasia here, where there's an expansion. There's a little bit of loss of tissue architecture. The cells look a bit different. And you see that you have more angiogenesis going on here. And here you have dysplasia. Here's the basement membrane still. And you have a lot of angiogenesis that's going on underneath the basement membrane. This is not invasive. The basement membrane is intact, but you have a lot of angiogenesis that's going on. Right? So just to show you here as well in cancers, here you have an in-situ prostate cancer, an in-situ breast cancer, and you see that the angiogenesis is occurring right around the perimeter here, but not going through the basement membrane, as opposed to when there is an invasive breast cancer. And you can see that there's lots of angiogenesis that's occurring through the depth of this whole tumor. Right? So this angiogenesis happens a lot sooner than in a benign or a pre-malignant state. Okay? And what is the determinant in the tissue? Well, there's this balancing act of angiogenesis. Very similar to the balancing act for the cell to decide on apoptosis. It's how many activators are there in relation to the concentration of inhibitors. So that balancing act. So if there are more activators, you end up with angiogenesis. If there are more inhibitors, you end up with no angiogenesis. And so just to say that there are lots of anti-angiogenic drugs that are in use already, as this was touted by Judah Folkman as the answer to keeping cancers at bay. But obviously it's only now used in combination therapy. It's not the complete answer.
blocks.why: This section explains why expanding tumors require new blood vessel recruitment, the timing of the angiogenic switch, and the balance of pro- and anti-angiogenic signals.

blocks.label: Mechanisms, routes, and challenges of metastasis
blocks.content: Okay, so onto the last one. And I'll just have a sip of water. Which is metastasis, which is arguably the most important hallmark that we should be treating, because metastasis is responsible for most of the cancer deaths. Right? So unless it's a benign tumor in the brain, most of the death that we see is because of metastasis. So the question would be: What mutation can we attribute a metastatic capacity to? Therefore, we could go after that mutation or whatever that function or activity is with some inhibitors, with some drugs. If we could get the answer to that question of which gene should we go after or which protein should we go after, we would be able to treat 90% of the cancers. The problem is, is that nothing has really been found so far as a genetic signature for metastasis. So in the stepwise progression of when does the capacity for metastasis appear in this, we don't really have the answer to that question, and that's why there's a question mark still here. But we do know that the cancer cell has to go through this very large process of invading locally, getting into the tissue, or the vessels that are around, survive while it is in the circulation around in the blood or in the lymph, and then exit that circulation and then form these micrometastases in distant sites, and then survive. So, what is happening? There are a lot of different steps where the cancer cell has to survive. So clearly there has to have been a gain of a lot of functions to do this. So I have a little movie, which is here, to show you what this looks like. And this is on a loop because this is fun to watch. Which is the kind of migration that you can get in tissues, right? And you can see that the cells are very, very migratory and they all follow one another. And there's supposed to be this microvasculature that the cells are using to invade, to have a leading edge. And you have some cells that zip along, and you have other cells here that don't seem to be moving at all, and are actually getting pushed along by other cells. Whoops. Oh, well. Okay. Some laggards in the system there. But the point is that for a cell like that, one of the things that there's a little bit of controversy about invasiveness causing tissue damage. And in some cases it might be tissue damage, but in other cases, there's microvasculature that the cells could just walk through that are used by other, say for example, immune cells that wander through tissues, macrophages and things like that to get around. So in talking about how a cancer cell would get out of its primary site and access the circulation, we have here the example of a breast cancer, which would migrate into the lymphatics. And the draining lymphatics would drain into the venous system and then enter the heart, and the lungs, and then go around the arterial system. And so in that way would gain access to tissues kind of all around the body. So, in making a diagnosis, after you take that primary biopsy, what can be done is to try and figure out which is the sentinel lymph node that one would sample to understand whether or not this tumor has actually metastasized, entered the circulation. And that is normally done by injecting a dye and seeing which is the first lymph node to show up with the stain, and then that lymph node would be sampled. And then you would then look within the lymph node, via immunohistochemistry in this case, for a biomarker of the tumor. So as we know that this would be an epithelial tumor, you would look for epithelial markers. So in this case, cytokeratin. And so cytokeratin showing up in a lymph node is evidence that a cell of epithelial origin is somehow present in a lymph node, which means it's a bad sign. Which means that the tumor has left the primary site and entered into the lymphatics. Right? So the tumor cells leaving the primary site have to take advantage, or they do take advantage of the circulatory system that is present. So as you can see here, what this means is that a lot of these tumors that would arise in these tissues here, breast, muscle, skin, brain, and kidneys, would enter the venous circulation and then get trapped, perhaps in the microvasculature of the lungs before gaining access to the arterial circulation and then going around the body. Whereas, if the tumor was here in the pancreas, spleen, or in the gut, this would first access the portal system and get trapped in the liver, before then entering again more of the lymphatics and gaining access to the rest of the tissue. So there is a sense of where tumors might go, because of the normal circulatory system that exists. But obviously, because the tumors could theoretically go every and anywhere depending on this kind of circulation, it would be beneficial to be able to understand what the tumor load is like and whether it has metastasized by having a different kind of biomarker. And so this is what is done now in terms of circulating tumor cells. So these would be the biomarkers that people would choose as a liquid biopsy to monitor monitor the patient's treatment. So monitoring circulating tumor cells isn't really good as a population study, but it is good to measure in an individual longitudinally to understand whether or not treatments are working. So for example, if you have a low circulating tumor cell load prior to treatment and then that number decreases, that has the best prognosis for the patient. Whereas if you have a low number and nothing happens as a result of your treatment in terms of the circulating tumor cell level, that is a worse prognosis. Similarly, a high circulating tumor cell load that responds to treatment has a better prognosis than one that doesn't. Right? So it's a good way to track what's going on in terms of your treatment. Okay. So just to say that these metastatic cells that enter circulation have to do a lot of things in order to survive and become clinically detectable here at the end. So as I said, they have to go through these steps to get out of the circulation. First, they have to get in it, then they have to get out of it, and once they get out of it, they need to, as a single cell and potentially as a colony, they need to continue to proliferate until they become clinically detectable. At any of these stages, they may become dormant, they could become senescent, or they could die, or they could get treated. So any number of things could happen before they manage to become clinically detectable tumors. So there's a whole level of inefficiency in this process. So the number of tumor cells that are shed into the circulation is in vast excess to the number of cells that actually manage to survive and form a tumor. So the idea then is that there is a contribution, if you like, from the cancer cell itself and where it is going. So this idea of seed and soil. So the cancer cell itself and the secondary site have to be compatible in order for you to get this clinically detectable tumor. And those things that determine all of these factors are mechanical factors, so how the cell is circulating around the body. There's also things like tissue stiffness, cancer cell stiffness, and how many cells are being shed at any given time, and also the soil in terms of the specific environment that's provided by that tumor. So all of these things together contribute as to whether or not metastasis actually occurs. So again, we're going back to that question of is there a gene? Is there something that we can go after? And unfortunately, as I said, there's been a lot of sequencing studies done to sequence both the primary tumor and the secondary metastases to see, well, what is the change that occurred from one to the other? And unfortunately, the answer to that, there isn't an easy answer to that because what you see in the metastases is that they are clonal derivatives of that primary tumor. So you'll end up with the majority of them have exactly the same driver mutations, and they are to the tune of 96%, if you like, and they also have the same biallelic inactivation of tumor suppressor genes. So what you're looking at is a clone that's managed to survive elsewhere. The biggest signature that we have is whole genome duplication. Right? And whole genome duplication just means that kind of aneuploidy that we saw at the very, very beginning. So if we go back to our stepwise progression of accumulating different mutations that end up causing you to go from normal to a carcinoma, that chromosomal instability that we talked about in the last lecture is a big, if you like, precursor to becoming capable, theoretically, of getting to that metastatic state. So it probably means that you have a lot more genetic material to play with, and if you have a lot more genetic material to play with, you have more cards and pathways at your disposal to live in all these different places. So you have a lot of luggage. So lots of different things that you could do.
blocks.why: This section discusses the multi-step invasion-metastasis cascade, anatomical circulatory routes, circulating tumor cell monitoring, and the genetic complexity of secondary colonization.

blocks.label: Concluding summary and recommended reading
blocks.content: So what I also wanted to say and just finish on in terms of how the hallmark papers all end is to say that pretty much the route to cancer can be very, very different for everybody in terms of which mutations show up, which hallmarks are showing up and when, and which mutations are responsible for taking you to this kind of cancerous state. But at the end, when all of the cancers are considered together, these hallmarks are pretty much showing up all together. And just in case you didn't have enough of the hallmarks, Doug Hanahan actually published this paper last year to talk about going beyond the hallmarks. But I have to say that I have never seen a review that has had sentences that are all 30 words long. So if you want to get into conceptually distinct but interconnected parametric dimensions of the hallmarks, I invite you to read this. However, I would be more than happy if you just ended up with this at the end of this lecture, which is to be able to identify them, as we said, and explain how these mutations work and how the hallmarks work. Okay? All right. And I'm happy to take any questions, and I will see you in the practicals.
blocks.why: The lecturer concludes the lecture by summarizing how cancer hallmarks converge, mentioning recent literature expansions, and closing the session.
